# Pedro F. Rackebrandt: research in full

> Every paper summary from https://rackebrandt.pe/, as plain text.

## When regimes cycle

Pedro F. Rackebrandt, 2026. Working paper. Topic: Regimes. Tags: Nonlinear dynamics, Political economy, V-Dem. Page: https://rackebrandt.pe/papers/when-regimes-cycle/

Many countries swing between democracy and autocracy for decades. Polybius called it anacyclosis. In my model the swings need no run of bad luck: the economy decides when they start and when they stop.

One quantity does the work: the pool of young people free to be mobilized. Below a threshold, a shock sets off swings that shrink each round. Above it, the swings never die out and the country keeps cycling. Falling behind your neighbours fills the pool and lifts a country over. A crisis erodes institutions and drops it back below.

Three predictions follow. Young autocracies that fall behind their neighbours open up. Crises keep autocracies shut and break young democracies. New autocracies often fall when a neighbour turns democratic, until they consolidate. All three hold in V-Dem data from 1950 to 2019, under eight different codings of regime type.

How to read the figure:

One flat axis runs from closed to open rule; the other is how mobilized people are. Height is the pool of young people, and the dashed square marks the threshold. The blue line is the country’s path and the red dot is where it stands now.

The arrows step through three stories. On the last slide you run the country yourself. Drag the figure to rotate it.

::: short
- Countries can swing between open and closed rule on their own. No run of bad luck is needed.
- One quantity decides whether the swings fade or last: the pool of young people free to mobilize. Below a threshold, shocks die out. Above it, the swings never stop.
- The economy moves countries across that threshold. Falling behind the neighbours pushes them over; a crisis pulls them back. All three predictions hold in data on nearly every country from 1950 to 2019.
:::

[[figure]]

### The puzzle

Many countries swing between democracy and autocracy for decades. Polybius called it anacyclosis. The usual story blames bad luck: a coup here, a crash there. But the swings look too regular for luck. Is there an engine?

### Two forces

The model follows two quantities, each measured from where the country would settle if left alone.

- **Mobilization** $m$: how many people are organized against the rulers. It feeds on a pool of young people free to be mobilized. The size of that pool is $K$.
- **Inclusiveness** $x$: how far the elite opens institutions to absorb opponents, with seats, jobs and a say.

Opening up has a payoff and a price. Each opponent absorbed is worth $v$ to the elite. Keeping institutions open costs $c\eta$. Absorbing also takes time, $h$ per activist, so institutions can take in at most $1/h$ activists at once.

> Openness survives only if $v > c\eta$: an absorbed opponent must be worth more than keeping the doors open. Otherwise inclusiveness dies out, whatever the starting point.

### The loop

The two forces chase each other round a circle.

<svg class="loop" viewBox="0 0 360 222" role="img" aria-label="The loop: mobilization builds, the elite opens up, activists are absorbed and mobilization falls, openness stops paying and the elite closes, then mobilization builds again."><defs><marker id="loop-head" viewBox="0 0 8 8" refX="6.5" refY="4" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path class="loop-tip" d="M0,0 L8,4 L0,8 z"/></marker></defs><path class="loop-arc" d="M198.7,44.6 A68,68 0 0 1 245.4,91.3" marker-end="url(#loop-head)"/><path class="loop-arc" d="M245.4,128.7 A68,68 0 0 1 198.7,175.4" marker-end="url(#loop-head)"/><path class="loop-arc" d="M161.3,175.4 A68,68 0 0 1 114.6,128.7" marker-end="url(#loop-head)"/><path class="loop-arc" d="M114.6,91.3 A68,68 0 0 1 161.3,44.6" marker-end="url(#loop-head)"/><text x="180" y="30" text-anchor="middle">Mobilization builds</text><text x="258" y="114" text-anchor="start">Elite opens up</text><text x="180" y="198" text-anchor="middle">Activists absorbed,</text><text x="180" y="212" text-anchor="middle">mobilization falls</text><text x="102" y="100" text-anchor="end">Openness no</text><text x="102" y="114" text-anchor="end">longer pays,</text><text x="102" y="128" text-anchor="end">elite closes</text><text class="loop-mid" x="180" y="106" text-anchor="middle">fed by the</text><text class="loop-mid" x="180" y="120" text-anchor="middle">pool K</text></svg>

1. Young people join, and mobilization builds.
2. The elite opens up, because absorbing opponents pays.
3. Absorption drains mobilization.
4. With few opponents left, openness stops paying and institutions close.
5. The pool refills, and mobilization builds again.

This is the logic of predator and prey in ecology, the Rosenzweig and MacArthur model. Activists are the prey and open institutions the predator.

### Fade or cycle?

Each turn of the loop is either a little smaller than the last or the same size. The size of the pool decides which:

$$K^* = \frac{1}{h} + 2m^*$$

Here $m^*$ is mobilization at the resting point.

::: intuition
A small pool behaves like a pendulum with friction: push it and it swings, but each swing is smaller than the last. A large pool behaves like a clock: mobilization surges faster than institutions can absorb it, overshoots, and the swing never dies. Ecologists call this the paradox of enrichment: feed a pond and predator and prey start to boom and bust.
:::

- **Below $K^*$**, a shock sets off loops that shrink. A new regime is safest at first and most at risk when the first swing comes back.
- **Above $K^*$**, the resting point breaks and a lasting cycle appears. Mathematicians call this a Hopf bifurcation.

Near the threshold every such cycle looks alike. Write $r$ for the distance from the resting point:

$$\dot r = \mu\, r - r^3, \qquad \mu \propto K - K^*$$

When $\mu < 0$, every loop shrinks back to $r = 0$. When $\mu > 0$, small loops grow until the $r^3$ term stops them at $r = \sqrt{\mu}$. So cycles are born small, and their size grows with $\sqrt{K - K^*}$.

### What moves a country across

- **Falling behind the neighbours** fills the pool and raises $K$. A calm autocracy can tip into the loop and start to open.
- **A crisis** speeds the erosion of institutions and drops the country below the threshold. The loop shuts, and a young democracy can close with it.
- **A neighbour turning democratic** pulls a new autocracy toward reopening, until the autocracy consolidates.

### The evidence

The tests use V-Dem, which scores nearly every country's regime each year, from 1950 to 2019. They are repeated under eight different codings of regime type. All three predictions hold:

1. Young autocracies that fall behind their neighbours open up.
2. Crises keep autocracies shut and break young democracies.
3. New autocracies often fall when a neighbour turns democratic, until they consolidate.

### Why it matters

Regime change need not be an accident. The economy decides which side of $K^*$ a country sits on, so the same country can be stable in one decade and cycling in the next. Any shock, a new technology included, matters through two levers: whether absorbing opponents still pays ($v$ against $c\eta$), and how fast institutions can absorb them ($h$, and with it $K^*$).

## How many tests was it really?

Pedro F. Rackebrandt, Sebastian Winzker, 2026. Working paper. Topic: Finance. Tags: Deflated Sharpe, Quantitative Finance. Page: https://rackebrandt.pe/papers/how-many-tests/

Why does this matter? When you test thousands of trading rules, the best one will look good by chance. Cluster corrections that group similar rules can make noise look significant by undercounting the tests. A block bootstrap on the real grid keeps the correlations and shows the safer hurdle is the full nominal count.

We resample the 2,825 moving average rules together. On the DAX the effective independent tests are about 1,400. Correlation spread evenly barely lowers that number; only rules bunched in blocks do. The best rule still fails the hurdle on the DAX.

How to read the figure:

The curve is the expected maximum Sharpe ratio if every rule is noise. It grows like the square root of log N, so only the order of magnitude of N matters. The buttons read the hurdle at the cluster, effective, and nominal counts.

Software that clusters similar moving averages reports N = 2. That point sits far below the measured hurdle. The measured effective count is about 1,400. Using the raw grid of 2,825 overstates the hurdle by 6 percent.

On the DAX the best rule clears the mean of the noise maximum and still fails the 95 percent band.

::: short
- Try enough trading rules and the best one will look good by pure luck. The bar a rule must clear has to rise with the number of rules tried.
- Similar rules are not independent tests, and some software counts a grid of 2,825 moving averages as just 2. We measure the real count with a bootstrap: about 1,400 on the DAX.
- Undercounting cuts the bar by up to 84 percent and calls noise a discovery. Using the full count overstates it by only 6 percent. When in doubt, count every rule.
:::

[[figure]]

### The problem

Give 2,825 traders a coin each and let them trade the DAX by its flips. One of them will post a superb record. Testing a grid of moving average rules plays the same game: the best rule's record is partly luck, and the more rules you try, the more luck the best one carries.

### The bar set by luck

How good does the best of $N$ worthless strategies look on average? Bailey and López de Prado (2014) give the answer:

$$\begin{aligned} \widehat{SR}_0 = \mathrm{E}\Big[\max_n \widehat{SR}_n\Big] \approx \sigma_{SR}\Big[&(1-\gamma)\,\Phi^{-1}\Big(1-\frac{1}{N}\Big) \\ &+\gamma\,\Phi^{-1}\Big(1-\frac{1}{N e}\Big)\Big] \end{aligned}$$

$\widehat{SR}_n$ is the measured Sharpe ratio of rule $n$ and $\sigma_{SR}$ how much those ratios vary across rules. $\Phi^{-1}$ turns a probability into a normal quantile, $\gamma \approx 0.5772$ is the Euler Mascheroni constant and $e$ is Euler's number.

::: intuition
The best of many draws creeps up slowly. In the figure's calibration, the bar is 0.05 with 2 rules, 0.30 with 1,000 and 0.35 with 10,000. It grows like $\sqrt{\ln N}$, so the order of magnitude of $N$ is what matters. Counting 2 instead of 1,400 changes everything; counting 2,825 instead of 1,400 changes little.
:::

A rule convinces only if it clears this bar with room to spare. The deflated Sharpe ratio turns "room to spare" into a probability:

$$\mathrm{DSR} = \Phi\!\left(\frac{\big(\widehat{SR}-\widehat{SR}_0\big)\sqrt{T-1}}{\sqrt{1-\hat{S}\,\widehat{SR}+\dfrac{\hat{K}-1}{4}\,\widehat{SR}^{2}}}\right)$$

The top is the margin over luck, scaled up by the length of the record, $T$ returns. The bottom is how noisy a Sharpe ratio is: skew $\hat S$ and fat tails $\hat K$ (3 for normal returns) make it noisier. A DSR near 1 means the margin is too large to be luck.

### How many tests is a grid?

A 50 day and a 51 day moving average trade almost the same way. So 2,825 rules are fewer than 2,825 independent tests. How many fewer?

We let the data answer. A stationary block bootstrap reshuffles the market's own history in blocks of about ten trading days and runs every rule on the same reshuffled days, so the rules stay as similar as they really are. Each reshuffle shows how good the best rule looks in a world with no skill. The effective number of tests $N_{\text{eff}}$ is the count of independent rules that would produce the same average best:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{E}^{*}\Big[\max_n \widehat{SR}_n\Big] = \sigma_{SR}\Big[&(1-\gamma)\,\Phi^{-1}\Big(1-\frac{1}{N_{\text{eff}}}\Big) \\ &+\gamma\,\Phi^{-1}\Big(1-\frac{1}{N_{\text{eff}}\,e}\Big)\Big] \end{aligned}$$

$\mathrm{E}^{*}$ is the average over reshuffles. The right side rises with $N_{\text{eff}}$, so exactly one count fits.

### The result

| Count | $N$ | Bar set by luck |
|---|---|---|
| Clustering software | 2 | 0.05 |
| Bootstrap, DAX | about 1,400 | 0.31 |
| Every rule | 2,825 | 0.33 |

The cluster count cuts the bar by 84 percent and lets noise pass as skill. The full count overstates it by 6 percent.

::: intuition
Why do similar rules still count as so many tests? A move shared by every rule lifts or sinks the whole grid together, so it never singles out a winner. Luck enters through the ways rules differ, and those differences stay many. Only rules locked together in tight blocks act as one test.
:::

Of the standard corrections based on eigenvalues of the correlation matrix, only Gao (2008) comes close. What moves the Sharpe ratio a rule must beat:

| Source | Effect |
|---|---|
| Trying many rules | factor of 7.3 |
| $N_{\text{eff}}$ in place of $N$ | minus 3.1 percent |
| Daily returns not being normal | plus 0.2 percent |

The best moving average rule survives in 3 of 17 markets and 2 of 31 German stocks. On the DAX it beats the average luck of the best noise rule and fails the 95 percent band.

### Why it matters

The two errors are not symmetric. Counting too many tests costs a few percent of the bar; counting too few can wipe out most of it. So the safe default is the plain count of every rule you tried.

## Reversed by our own replication

Pedro F. Rackebrandt, 2026. Working paper. Topic: AI. Tags: Verification, Multi model. Page: https://rackebrandt.pe/papers/reversed-by-replication/

Why does this matter? An automated auditor that checks research extractions is right only about a third of the time, yet a wrong extraction can still return a theorem. We registered three signals in advance that might catch the error, then tested them once on frontier models. Two reversed. Cross model disagreement is the one that held.

On 174 items, a model disagreeing with its own repeats cleared the bar in only one family. Disagreement across models reached 0.75 and stayed above the threshold. It flagged errors better on unconventional designs. Abstaining where models disagree most trims the error rate from 81% to 72%, but the tool remains weak.

How to read the figure:

Each row is a registered comparison. The open square is the discovery sample on five open weight arms. The filled circle is the confirmatory run on four frontier families. The dashed navy line is the 0.65 threshold we deposited before seeing those families. The dotted line is chance.

Task structure falls from 0.771 to about 0.50 and is retracted. Within model sampling falls from 0.727 and clears the bar in one family of four. Cross model disagreement rises from 0.609 to 0.753 and is held.

::: short
- Language models now read research papers and write down their causal design. Most of these readings are wrong, and a wrong reading still produces a confident result further down the line.
- Can we tell which readings to distrust without an answer key? We fixed three warning signals in advance and tested them once on four frontier model families.
- Two signals reversed. One held: when different model families disagree about a case, their reading is more likely wrong. Skipping the most disputed half cuts the error rate from 81 to 72 percent.
:::

[[figure]]

### The problem

A causal claim stands on its design: what was treated, what was measured, what was held fixed. Given that design, algorithms (Shpitser and Pearl; Jaber et al.) decide mechanically whether the effect can be identified. The weak link is the step before: reading the paper into a design. Language models now do that reading. Most of their readings fail the benchmark's grader, and a wrong reading still returns a verdict.

### The idea

::: intuition
Ask three people to summarise a paper. If they disagree, at least one of them is wrong. Disagreement is a warning light that needs no answer key.
:::

Three candidate lights:

- **Within model disagreement** $d^{W,f}_i$: ask one model family $f$ three times about item $i$ and see how much its answers differ.
- **Cross model disagreement** $d^{C}_i$: ask four different families and see how much they differ.
- **Task structure** $k^f_i$: count the design fields in the answer. More fields, more room for error.

### The test

Five open weight models served as the discovery sample and picked out the three signals. The decision rules were then registered on OSF on 13 September 2026, with the hash of the analysis script deposited, and run once on four frontier families: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and xAI. Each answered every item three times at temperature 1.0, 2,088 readings in all.

The items are the 174 cases of CausalReasoningBenchmark (Sawarni, Tan, Syrgkanis), each with an expert design. The authors' grader, `evaluate_identification`, checks each family's most frequent answer. The error $e^f_i$ is 1 when it fails and 0 when it passes.

A signal $s$ is scored by its AUROC, written $A(s)$:

$$A(s) = \Pr\big(s_i > s_j \mid e_i = 1,\ e_j = 0\big)$$

::: intuition
Pick one wrong reading and one right reading at random. $A(s)$ is the chance the signal flags the wrong one as more suspicious, with ties counted as half. A coin flip scores 0.5; a perfect signal scores 1.
:::

The registered bar was 0.65. With $f$ running over the four families, the rules were:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{C1:}&\quad \#\{f : A(d^{W,f}) \ge 0.65\} \ge 3 \\ \text{C2:}&\quad A(d^{C}) \ge 0.65 \\ \text{C3:}&\quad \#\{f : A(k^{f}) > A(d^{W,f})\} \ge 3 \end{aligned}$$

### The result

| Signal | Discovery | Frontier | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| C1 Within model | 0.727 | 0.680, Google only | Failed |
| C2 Cross model | 0.609 | 0.753, interval [0.661, 0.840] | Held |
| C3 Task structure | 0.771 | about 0.50, one family | Retracted |

The signal ranked last in discovery is the only one that survived. Disagreement inside one family says little about its errors; disagreement between families tracks them.

A registered falsifier predicted the opposite on unusual designs: families would agree on the same wrong answer. Disagreement flagged errors better there, 0.868 against 0.646, with a permutation $p = 0.025$. Neither the number of families nor how accurate they are explains the reversal.

Skipping the half of the items with the most cross model disagreement lowers the error on what is kept:

$$\bar e_{\text{all}} = 80.9\% \;\longrightarrow\; \bar e_{\text{kept}} = 72.4\%$$

### Why it matters

Two lessons. Cross model disagreement is a cheap, honest warning light for automated reading of research. But it is no fix: the half it keeps is still wrong 72 percent of the time, so the reading step itself needs work. And registering the rules in advance mattered. On discovery data alone, two of the three signals would have been reported as findings.
